title: Skip check: can you leave this section?

what.md: This section taught five things. If you can do all five unaided, skip ahead — nothing later depends on a definition you already hold.

items: State what a graph is and why it is stored as a matrix rather than a picture.
Say what the degree of a vertex is, and why the degrees of a graph sum to twice the number of edges.
Build the incidence matrix of a hypergraph, given the vertex list and the hyperedge list.
Read the two degrees off that matrix — row sums and column sums — and check one against the other.
Explain why convolution does not transfer to graphs without modification.

what.md: The questions below are the check. Two of the four correct is not the bar — the bar is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If you hesitated on the incidence matrix, stay: card 3's matrix is Equation (3)'s raw material.

quiz.q: Which quantity does the *column* sum of an incidence matrix give?

opts.md: The vertex degree — how many hyperedges contain a vertex
opts.expl: That is the row sum. Getting these two the wrong way round is the single most common error with this matrix, and it silently swaps Table I's two degree columns.

opts.md: The edge degree — how many vertices a hyperedge contains
opts.expl: Correct: the size of the relation. For a plain graph every column sum is 2, which is why Table I prints 2 for all four graph datasets.
That is the sum of all column sums, or equivalently of all row sums — the whole matrix, not one column.

quiz.q: A hypergraph has 50 vertices, 10 hyperedges, and 400 total memberships. What is its average edge degree?
quiz.hint: Memberships divided by hyperedges — the column-sum direction.
quiz.sol: $400 \div 10 = 40$ vertices per hyperedge on average. For contrast, the average vertex degree would be $400 \div 50 = 8$.

quiz.q: Why must every graph operator give the same answer regardless of how the vertices are ordered?

opts.md: Because the ordering is part of the data and must be respected
opts.expl: The ordering is an artefact of how the file happened to be written. No dataset comes with a meaningful numbering, and the paper's permutation-invariance lemma exists precisely because of that.

opts.md: Because the ordering is arbitrary, so any answer depending on it is an artefact rather than a property of the graph
opts.expl: Correct. The graph is the connections; the numbering is bookkeeping. This is the intuition behind the paper's column-exchange invariance proof, which shows its structural encoder satisfies exactly this requirement.

opts.md: Because the Laplacian requires sorted indices
opts.expl: The Laplacian is defined for any ordering — its entries move with the labels, and its eigenvalues do not.

quiz.q: Why does repeatedly averaging a signal over neighbours destroy information rather than spread it?

opts.md: Because averaging is not a valid operation on graphs
opts.expl: It is perfectly valid — and it is what makes GNNs work at all. The problem is applying it too many times, not applying it.

opts.md: Because each round replaces every value with a blend of its neighbourhood, so differences shrink towards zero
opts.expl: Correct. A few rounds propagate information usefully; many rounds make every vertex look like the graph average, leaving nothing to classify. The paper's Table VIII measures exactly this collapse in the baseline.

opts.md: Because averaging loses the highest-frequency signal components
opts.expl: Closer to the spectral view of the phenomenon, and true as far as it goes — but the mechanism that matters for reading this paper is the direct one: values converge to the same number.

close: **You are ready for the paper's own objects.** The hypergraph pair follows, and it assumes everything in this section. If you skipped, you will meet the incidence matrix again in Equation (3) — come back then.
